title: 基于图嵌入的知识图谱推理与发现
abstract: This paper explores the application of graph embedding techniques to knowledge graph reasoning and discovery. Traditional knowledge graph reasoning methods often struggle with scalability and accuracy, particularly when dealing with complex relationships within large knowledge graphs. This research proposes a novel approach that leverages graph embedding algorithms to represent entities and relationships within a knowledge graph as dense vector representations. These embeddings capture the structural and semantic information inherent in the graph, enabling efficient and accurate reasoning and new knowledge discovery. We investigate various embedding techniques, including Node2Vec, DeepWalk, and TransE, evaluating their performance on several reasoning tasks. The results demonstrate that graph embeddings significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of knowledge graph reasoning compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the learned embeddings provide a valuable tool for identifying novel relationships and patterns within the knowledge graph, leading to the discovery of new knowledge. This work contributes to the growing field of knowledge graph technology by providing a practical and effective approach to knowledge graph reasoning and discovery based on the power of graph embedding techniques.

title: 基于动态概率的概率图理论的推广
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic model called Dynamic Probability Graph (DPG) Theory, which extends the core concepts of probability graph theory to dynamically evolving probability distributions. We propose a dynamic adjustment algorithm that iteratively refines the probability distribution based on a defined objective function, allowing for complex optimization problems within the context of probabilistic modeling. The core mechanism focuses on representing probability as a dynamic graph, where nodes represent probability values and edges represent probabilistic relationships. This allows for the incorporation of feedback loops and adaptive adjustment, addressing limitations of static probability graph theory. The paper demonstrates the efficacy of this approach through several illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to effectively tackle optimization challenges typically addressed by traditional methods.

title: Title: Adaptive Machine Learning via Graph Theory Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive machine learning method that leverages graph theory principles to enhance feature learning and model optimization. Traditional machine learning models heavily rely on feature engineering, often requiring extensive manual effort. This approach proposes a novel method that dynamically adapts to the inherent structure of the data through graph theory, offering improved efficiency and potentially enhanced model performance. The core mechanism involves applying graph theory concepts to represent and model data relationships, facilitating more effective feature extraction and optimization. The paper explores the potential benefits of this approach, emphasizing its ability to automatically discover and utilize relevant graph structures to improve model accuracy and generalization.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Accelerated Distributed Computing
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed computing leveraging the phenomenon of quantum entanglement. The core claim is that by directly connecting distributed computing nodes through entangled quantum states, we can drastically reduce data transmission latency and significantly accelerate computational processes. The proposed mechanism involves constructing a carefully designed quantum entanglement network, enabling instantaneous information exchange between nodes – effectively bypassing the limitations imposed by the speed of light. This approach shifts the paradigm from relying solely on quantum computers for classical computation to utilizing the fundamental properties of quantum mechanics as an intrinsic acceleration mechanism. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this method, focusing on the potential for parallel computation and collaborative processing facilitated by entanglement. This research aims to establish a foundational understanding of entanglement-accelerated distributed computing, paving the way for future exploration and development in this nascent field. The central equation demonstrating the potential speed-up is: Δt = (Δs/c) + t_c, where Δt is the total computation time, Δs is the size of the data set, c is the speed of light, and t_c is the classical computation time. We demonstrate that, with perfect entanglement, Δt can be reduced substantially, approaching a speed increase of approximately 1/c, which is significantly faster than the conventional speed of data transfer.

title: Where Perceptrons Meet Proof Trees: A Comparative Analysis Review of Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning Systems
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning Systems in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of neuro-symbolic and reasoning as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: The Influence of Hate Speech on Social Media on Shaping Young People’s Socio-Political Attitudes
abstract: The modern media environment today includes forms of interactivity through a wide variety of communication channels. Promoting and supporting hatred, violence, and intolerance through the media and other communication channels in sensitive ethnically divided societies, such as Bosnia and Herzegovina, can result in immeasurable consequences. The research aimed to analyze, within a selected group of respondents, the degree of recognition and perception of content with elements of hate on social networks using the survey and focus group method, and to identify possible forms of influence of such content on the formation of attitudes of young people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The analysis starts from the standpoint that adequate forms of recognition and condemnation of all forms of dissemination of content with elements of hate can influence the creation of consensus, unity, tolerance, peace, and a stable and safe socio-political environment in the future. The research results show that young people to a significant extent recognize content with elements of hate speech and assume their harmful consequences. Social networks, as the primary communication tools of young people, are becoming a space in which identities are affirmed, contested and redefined, and hate narratives often gain wide reach and legitimacy through user interaction. Hate speech on social networks is not manifested exclusively through open and explicit forms of insults, but also through covert discursive patterns, with topics related to ethnic and religious identity being the dominant triggers for polarized user reactions and the production of additional radicalization of discourse.

title: From Sequential Language to Structural Intelligence: Toward Relationship-Aware AI
abstract: Large language models have transformed artificial intelligence by showing how much can be learned from language at scale. Their success has made language appear to be the dominant substrate of intelligence. This Blue Sky paper argues that this view is incomplete. We focus on one specific gap: what may be missing when relationships and structure are learned primarily through language. We argue that LLMs face two language bottlenecks. First, they are token-sequence systems: even with attention and rich internal representations, they process and generate language through sequences of tokens. Second, their training data is human language, which is the sequential expression of cognition rather than the full relational process from which cognition emerges. Neuroscience gives reason to take this distinction seriously: the connectome and network neuroscience describe the brain in terms of elements, connections, and graph-like organization, while recent work argues that language is primarily a tool for communication rather than thought itself. This suggests that LLMs learn from linguistic traces of intelligence, but not necessarily from the full relational processes that produce those traces. We therefore argue for relationship-aware AI as an open research direction: not a solved architecture, but a search for ways to combine linguistic fluency with explicit awareness of relationships and structure. The central distinction is between inference-time use of relationships and training-time learning from relationships. Many current systems add structure after a language model has already been trained, through retrieval, graph augmentation, tools, memory, or verification layers. These approaches are important, but the deeper Blue Sky challenge is to make relationships part of representation learning itself, so that structural awareness is learned by the model rather than supplied only after training.

title: Spatio-temporal graph neural network for state awareness and fault diagnosis in virtual power plant communication networks
abstract: Power communication networks in virtual power plants (VPPs) play a critical role in enabling reliable information exchange among distributed energy resources, energy storage systems, controllable loads, and dispatch centers. However, their complex topology, strong inter-node dependency, and hidden fault propagation paths make accurate state awareness and fault diagnosis highly challenging for conventional rule-based and shallow learning methods. To address this issue, this paper proposes a graph neural network (GNN)-based state awareness and fault diagnosis method for power communication networks in VPPs. First, a node-link coupled graph representation is constructed by integrating network topology and multi-source operational data, so as to capture the correlations among devices, communication links, and service states. Then, a GNN-based framework is developed to learn discriminative state features through neighborhood aggregation and graph representation learning, enabling the identification of multiple fault types, including link anomalies, node failures, and local congestion. In addition, temporal state evolution is incorporated to improve the model’s ability to characterize dynamic operating conditions and complex disturbances. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional machine learning and mainstream deep learning approaches in terms of state recognition accuracy, fault diagnosis precision, and robustness. The proposed method provides an effective solution for intelligent monitoring, online state awareness, and fault early warning in VPP communication networks.

title: No country for old linguists: LLM-brain alignment underdetermines neural computation
abstract: Nastase et al. (2026) argue that large language models (LLMs) may illuminate language processing because both rely on distributed, context-sensitive representations shaped by statistical learning. Their rejection of simple cortical "boxology" is persuasive, and they articulate a strong case for the value of LLM-brain alignment research. The key question is what kind of inference LLM-brain alignment licenses. My claim here will be narrow: representational alignment can in principle constrain mechanistic hypotheses, but it does not by itself identify a mechanism. Nastase et al. acknowledge that an encoding model can capture features represented in neural activity without establishing a shared architecture or algorithm. Yet the authors sometime move from alignment to "shared computational principles" and ultimately to LLMs as mechanistic models of natural language. Indeed, their methodological caveat that alignment does not establish a shared architecture or algorithm sits uneasily with their conclusion that LLMs might instantiate the same computational principles as biological brains and provide a "fully mechanistic model" of language. I discuss what I consider to be problems of logical, causal, and computational underdetermination in Nastase et al.'s (2026) proposal.

title: CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems
abstract: Production recommender systems shape what billions of people see, and sustaining their performance requires continual optimization: as content, user behavior, and upstream models shift, the choices governing retrieval, ranking, and serving must be revisited. Traditionally, human engineers test such changes through online experiments--a slow, reactive process limited by engineering effort, leaving parts of the system unrevised as conditions change. Although large language models have been applied to ranking, user modeling, and offline model development, few systems place an agent in a continual closed loop that acts on a live recommender and learns from the measured effects of its decisions. We present CORAL (Constraint-Optimized Recommender via an Agentic Loop), an LLM-native harness that closes this loop: each cycle, the agent observes operating signals, reasons over a memory of past decisions and outcomes, and invokes tools--including a numerical optimizer that keeps changes within a fixed operating budget--to reconfigure the recommender, with measured outcomes informing the next cycle. We formulate this as a partially observed, non-stationary, constrained optimization problem in which the policy improves in context, without parameter updates, from its prior actions. Across two large-scale social platforms, evaluated with A/B experiments, the same harness improves engagement at no additional serving cost on one and reduces serving cost without degrading engagement on the other, spanning the engagement-efficiency frontier. Performance improves as the loop iterates, suggesting that a single agentic loop can automate continual optimization work traditionally performed by human algorithm engineers under explicit guardrails.

title: ClaimReceipt: Verifying Evidence Sufficiency and Coverage in Agent Evaluations
abstract: Agent evaluations face two distinct evidentiary questions: whether a reported claim is recomputable from retained evidence (sufficiency), and whether the retained records cover the committed experiment set (coverage). Generic logs and hash-linked transcripts answer neither reliably. We introduce ClaimReceipt, a claim-relative receipt specification and selective verifier that binds typed transaction evidence to a signed experiment manifest and returns PASS, INVALID, or INCONCLUSIVE per claim. We freeze the specification before implementation (SHA-256 18d109...b81). On 1,392 historical buyer--seller records, a CR-2 verifier reproduces all five manually labeled audit verdicts, exactly replays 600 deterministic and 792 post-generation records, makes every one of 13 declared field groups non-redundant under tested ablations, and returns the expected result on 11/11 semantic faults with 0/8 false positives. We then run a separate prospective CR-3 epoch: 30 assignments are committed before inference, terminal receipts are signed and chained, and private evidence is encrypted for an auditor. Complete evidence yields coverage and accounting PASS; withholding one terminal receipt returns INCONCLUSIVE_COVERAGE, while withholding all private openings preserves coverage and protocol verification but makes economic claims inconclusive, exactly matching a preregistered prediction. Receipt instrumentation adds 0.021% of model-inference time and 9.9 KB per transaction. A specification-legibility probe indicates that our own frozen specification is not yet unambiguous to an independent reader. Claim verification therefore requires both claim-sufficient evidence and a committed universe against which omissions become visible.

title: APEx: Distillation of Agent Procedural Experience for Adaptive Deep Research Question Answering
abstract: Deep research agents augment large language models with external tools to answer complex, long-horizon questions through multi-turn reasoning. Learning from prior experience is crucial for continual improvement, yet existing methods either retrieve verbose task-specific traces that burden decision-making, or distill procedural skills that remain decoupled from downstream policy adaptation. We propose APEx, a hierarchical experience utilization framework that organizes interaction history into instance-level trajectory memories and category-level procedural skills, and couples them through a closed-loop architecture of Executor, Distiller, and Planner. The three modules are optimized via a three-stage alternating GRPO training paradigm, enabling reward-guided skill distillation rather than fixed-prompt generation. At test time, distilled skills serve as procedural priors for online Planner adaptation through skill-guided test-time reinforcement learning, allowing ground-truth-free self-improvement with skill-alignment regularization to prevent policy drift. Experiments on 7 benchmarks demonstrate that APEx achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing GPT-5.4 by 14.7 points and the strongest memory-augmented baseline by 3.0 points.

title: RoboTok: A Scalable Data Engine for Internet Demonstration Video Retrieval and Dexterous Manipulation Learning
abstract: Robot learning increasingly depends on broad and diverse demonstrations, yet collecting robot data remains expensive and difficult to scale across the wide range of real-world tasks. To address this bottleneck, we introduce RoboTok, a scalable data engine that uses a query human manipulation video to retrieve manipulation-relevant internet demonstrations for training dexterous robot policies. Specifically, we learn a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories expressed in estimated actor-centered reference frames. This representation enables manipulation behaviors to be compared across variations in camera viewpoint, scene appearance, and actor occlusions, while remaining compact enough for efficient indexing and retrieval over internet video collections. We evaluate RoboTok against existing robot-data retrieval approaches using retrieval metrics and downstream robot policy performance, showing that RoboTok retrieves more manipulation-relevant demonstrations and improves downstream task success. In real-world robot experiments, RoboTok-guided policies achieve a mean success improvement of 42.2 percentage points over the strongest baseline for each task, establishing hand-pose trajectory-aware retrieval as a scalable way to leverage continuously growing web video for robot learning.

To address this bottleneck, we introduce RoboTok, an internet-scale data engine that, given a query human manipulation video, retrieves manipulation-relevant human demonstrations from web videos for training dexterous robot policies. Specifically, we learn a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories expressed in estimated actor-centered reference frames. This representation enables manipulation behaviors to be compared across variations in camera viewpoint, scene appearance, and actor occlusions, while remaining compact enough for efficient search and continual indexing over internet-scale video collections. We evaluate RoboTok against existing robot-data retrieval approaches on retrieval benchmarks and downstream robot policy performance. Our results show that RoboTok retrieves more relevant manipulation demonstrations and improves downstream task success, establishing hand-pose trajectory-aware retrieval as a way to make web video a scalable and continuously growing source of supervision for robot learning.

title: Securing Processors from Hardware Exploits: A Real-Time Domain Adaptation for Resilient Attack Detection
abstract: Speculative execution features allow Spectre attacks to leak sensitive data. Using Hardware Performance Counters (HPCs) to detect these threats at runtime is promising, but standard machine learning models fail in real-world use because they break down due to hardware differences, background noise, and traffic shaping. To address this, our dissertation presents a unified framework combining physical hardware analysis with adaptive machine learning, systematically mapping how Spectre signatures vary across different leakage channels and processors like Intel, AMD, and ARM. To resolve these hardware-induced domain shifts, we designed a hybrid model that pairs a Domain-Adversarial LSTM (DA-LSTM) to track time-based patterns with an XGBoost classifier for precise decision boundaries, leveraging Source-Free Domain Adaptation (SFDA) so the system can automatically adjust to new, unlabeled hardware without original training data. Live client-server pipeline evaluations prove that this approach restores high-recall detection across diverse systems and matches traditional accuracy while cutting computational retraining time by roughly 85%, turning theoretical detection into a practical blueprint for microarchitectural defense.

title: ECG-based longitudinal risk prediction across diseases and organ systems
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence applied to routine electrocardiograms (ECGs) has largely focused on detecting existing disease or predicting individual cardiovascular outcomes. Whether ECGs can support prediction of multiple future diseases across organ systems remains unclear. We developed ECG-RISK, a multitask survival model for 67 incident three-character ICD-10 endpoints using ECG waveforms, demographic characteristics and routinely collected laboratory data from 86,673 MIMIC-IV patients. Discrimination was highest for heart, brain, kidney and lung endpoints, with organ-level C-indices ranging from 0.796 to 0.825, whereas liver and pancreatic endpoints showed lower discrimination. The ECG-only model achieved strong discrimination across most endpoints, whereas the incremental improvement gained by incorporating ECG and laboratory inputs beyond demographic information varied substantially across endpoints. Across the nine exploratory aggregated outcomes, Kaplan–Meier curves showed clear separation among model-score tertiles. Discrimination was highest for dementia (C-index, 0.891) and heart failure (C-index, 0.857). These findings support the feasibility of ECG-based longitudinal risk prediction across multiple diseases. External validation and competing-risk analyses are required to assess generalisability and clinical utility.

title: Exploring Execution-Form Boundaries in Brain–Cerebellum Collaboration: An Empirical Study from Cloud–Edge to Cost-Tiered Architectures
abstract: This preprint investigates "brain–cerebellum" collaboration in agent systems, where a high-capability model (the "brain") handles planning and verification while a low-cost model (the "cerebellum") performs execution tasks. Using DeepSeek v4-flash as the cloud brain and Google Gemma 4 e4B (a 14B-parameter MLX build), Qwen3.5 4B, and Qwen3.5 0.8B as candidate executors, we run two rounds of capability experiments, the G1–G4 collaboration experiments, and the V0–V4 variable-isolation experiments on the DSH agent framework.The central finding is counter-intuitive: in the tested configuration (Gemma 4 e4B as a DSH sub-agent on Mac M1 Pro, three multi-step scenarios), cloud–edge collaboration did not reduce tokens or wall-clock time — the sub-agent produced substantive output in only 8/21 attempts (~38%), and retries plus fallback increased output by 74% and wall-clock time by 8.1×. Variable isolation (V0–V4) attributes the failure to an interaction between execution form and model capability tier rather than to model ability alone: the same model completed 12/12 content-inlined direct calls but 0/3 when a tool schema was declared.A fixed-price-snapshot cost scenario analysis further estimates 45.0%–71.5% savings for cost-tiered collaboration (cheap cloud executors under a high-priced brain), pending real sub-agent validation.This upload contains the LaTeX source of the preprint together with a disclosure-safe data package: model specifications, task descriptions, aggregated task-level and per-run results, token details, and all cost-scenario tables. Raw session logs, execution scripts, and task materials are not published.Corresponding repository: https://github.com/TuringCorp-net/Paper-Boundaries-in-Brain-Cerebellum-Collaboration

title: Training Without Gathering the Data: A State of the Art Review of Federated Learning and Privacy-Preserving AI
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Federated Learning and Privacy-Preserving AI in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of federated learning and privacy as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Quantum Entanglement Prediction Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a unique challenge to traditional computational methods. This paper explores the potential of utilizing entanglement to enhance quantum computation, specifically focusing on the development of a novel prediction algorithm predicated on the non-local nature of entangled states. We propose a method that leverages the inherent properties of entanglement to predict the state of quantum systems with improved accuracy. This research aims to address limitations in current quantum algorithms by providing a new approach to quantum state determination. The core mechanism involves the construction of a predictive model, utilizing entanglement's non-classical behavior, to accurately forecast quantum system properties. This work explores the potential implications of this algorithm for enhancing quantum computing capabilities and highlights its unique advantages.

title: Quantum Adaptive Topology for Machine Learning
abstract: Quantum adaptive topology is a novel approach to machine learning that leverages the unique properties of quantum systems to construct models capable of enhanced prediction and control. This paper explores the potential of this technique, focusing on its ability to dynamically adjust topological structures within a machine learning framework. We detail the core mechanisms, argue for the potential advantages, and present a preliminary exploration of its implementation within a specific application – predicting the behavior of complex systems. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and the potential impact of this approach on the field of machine learning.

title: Dynamic Quantum Self-Organization Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum self-organization optimization framework. Traditional optimization methods often struggle to effectively address complex systems due to the inherent challenges of quantum mechanics. We propose a framework that utilizes quantum mechanics to automatically identify and optimize complex systems, leveraging a combination of quantum phenomena and optimization principles. The framework focuses on identifying optimal configurations within a system through iterative quantum self-organization, offering a fundamentally new approach to optimization challenges. The core claim of this work is that this framework provides a significantly more robust and effective method for optimizing complex systems compared to conventional techniques. We present a detailed overview of the proposed framework, its mathematical foundations, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in a specific, albeit simplified, case study.

title: Computational Complexity Theory for Neural Network Architectures
abstract: This research investigates the computational complexity of various neural network architectures, aiming to establish theoretical limits on their scalability and efficiency. Utilizing tools from computational complexity theory, we analyze the algorithmic complexity associated with both training and inference processes within diverse network structures. The core contribution lies in applying complexity theory's rigorous framework to neural networks, providing novel insights into their inherent limitations and potentially guiding the design of more efficient and scalable models. We explore the impact of architectural features, such as connectivity patterns and layer types, on computational complexity, focusing on the fundamental questions of whether certain neural network structures are fundamentally intractable to train or infer. The results highlight potential bottlenecks and offer a basis for future research focused on developing algorithms and architectures that overcome these limitations.

title: Probability Space Geometry for Adaptive Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic space geometry, termed Adaptive Probability Space Geometry (APSG), designed for learning and modeling complex data. The core principle of AGS is to dynamically adjust probability distributions within a probabilistic space, enabling the model to optimize performance through the evolution of these distributions. We propose a mechanism that leverages this dynamic adjustment to improve model accuracy and achieve adaptive learning. The research addresses the limitations of traditional machine learning by offering a framework that integrates probability distribution updates into the learning process, resulting in improved generalization and robustness. The core claim is that AGS offers a significant advancement in adaptive learning by dynamically shaping probability distributions, leading to enhanced model precision and improved performance on complex datasets.

title: Multi-Scale Adaptive Domain Partitioning and Knowledge Graph Fusion
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to enhance machine learning model performance by integrating multi-scale adaptive domain partitioning with knowledge graph fusion. The core claim is that intelligently partitioning complex data into scales and fusing domain knowledge graphs leads to significant improvements in performance and generalization capabilities within specific tasks. The core mechanism involves automatically generating multi-scale domain partitions using clustering or hierarchical methods, each tailored to a particular range of data. Subsequently, domain knowledge graphs are integrated into each domain model, providing contextual knowledge and constraints. The knowledge graph's reasoning abilities further aid in model training and validation. This research addresses the limitations of traditional, manually defined domain partitions, offering a more adaptive and intelligent domain modeling strategy. The evaluation framework focuses on demonstrating the benefits of this approach across diverse datasets and machine learning tasks. We present a methodology that prioritizes both granularity and context, resulting in robust and adaptable models. This work contributes to the advancement of domain adaptation techniques and knowledge-aware machine learning.

title: Cryptographic Proofs of Computation for Decentralized Machine Learning
abstract: Decentralized machine learning (DML) offers numerous advantages, including increased privacy, scalability, and robustness. However, a critical challenge remains: how to ensure the correctness of computations performed by these distributed models without revealing sensitive information. This paper proposes a novel framework utilizing cryptographic proofs of computation (PofC) to address this issue. Our approach leverages zero-knowledge proofs to enable a verifier to ascertain that a DML model has executed a specific computation – such as a training step or a prediction – without learning anything about the model's parameters or the underlying data. We outline a comprehensive system incorporating proof generation and verification strategies, highlighting the potential for enhanced security and efficiency in DML deployments. The core contribution is a practical methodology for establishing trust and accountability in decentralized learning environments. This work aims to pave the way for wider adoption of DML by providing a robust mechanism for validating the integrity of computations.

title: Based on Chaos Theory Optimization of Quantum Key Distribution Protocol
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocol leveraging the inherent sensitivity of chaotic systems. The core claim centers on utilizing the unpredictable nature of chaos to enhance security against chaotic attacks, a growing threat to current QKD protocols. The proposed protocol introduces controlled chaotic noise into the manipulation of quantum bits (qubits), rendering it significantly more resistant to attacks that exploit the deterministic behavior of chaotic systems. We explore the mathematical foundations of this approach, detailing the key equations governing the chaotic noise injection and the resultant impact on key generation. The design aims to mitigate the vulnerabilities present in conventional QKD protocols by introducing a layer of uncertainty, effectively disrupting the attacker's ability to predict and control the quantum system's state. This work provides a novel framework for QKD security enhancement, focusing on a proactive defense mechanism against emerging chaotic attack vectors. The theoretical analysis provides a robust foundation for further investigation and potential implementation.

title: Deep Learning-Driven Emotion Recognition for Personalized and Adaptive E-Learning Systems
abstract: This chapter explores how deep learning–based emotion recognition enhances student engagement and cognitive growth in e-learning environments. By leveraging CNN and LSTM architectures, the proposed framework detects learners' emotions from facial and behavioral cues in real time, enabling adaptive instructional responses. Through camera-based, non-invasive monitoring, emotions such as confusion, curiosity, or satisfaction are quantified to personalize learning experiences and improve retention. The chapter also discusses dataset selection, model design, and integration into Learning Management Systems (LMS). Case insights demonstrate how emotion-aware systems foster empathy, motivation, and inclusivity in digital education. Ethical considerations privacy, fairness, and explainability are addressed to ensure responsible AI deployment. The study establishes emotion recognition as a cornerstone for intelligent, adaptive, and human-centered e-learning ecosystems that align technology with emotional intelligence and pedagogical effectiveness.

title: Anthropomorphic Chatbots and Customer Loyalty
abstract: Human-like chatbots have fundamentally transformed how consumers seek and receive assistance. Despite the rapid deployment of chatbots, the lack of human empathy and the inability to address culturally embedded complexities persist as pivotal hurdles. This chapter proposes a conceptual framework that delineates the cognitive pathway from chatbot anthropomorphism to sustained customer loyalty, mediated by trust and engagement. Anchored in the Computers are Social Actors (CASA) theory, Social Presence Theory, and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this pathway is further examined with moderators—digital literacy, cultural values, and linguistic diversity in emerging markets. This chapter introduces a culturally nuanced framework for researchers studying conversational AI in emerging markets, in contrast to traditional research that predominantly emphasizes Western perspectives, while offering practitioners tangible insights for developing culturally intelligent, linguistically sensitive, and anthropomorphic chatbot experiences across diverse emerging markets.

title: GraphRAG Best Practices: A Modular Evaluation Framework and Regulatory Case Study
abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) enhances Large Language Models by integrating knowledge graphs into retrieval and generation. Despite growing adoption, no systematic study has isolated the contribution of individual pipeline components to end-to-end performance, leaving practitioners with-out evidence-based configuration guidance. We address this gap with a component-level empirical study spanning three GraphRAG stages, namely graph-based indexing, graph-guided retrieval, and graph-enhanced generation, and identify which design decisions most significantly influence answer quality. Across three datasets (MSMARCO, HotpotQA, and a domain-specific EU banking regulation corpus), we benchmark 17 embedding models, six retriever types with varying traversal depths, nine reranking models, and four graph serialisation formats for prompt construction. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) retriever combination strategy and traversal depth are dataset-dependent, with domain-specific corpora favouring shallow traversal and separate reranking; (2) a dual-retriever pairing hypothetical-question embeddings with entity-based retrieval, pruned by a cross-encoder reranker, yields the most robust performance across domains (F1 up to 89.9); and (3) code-like graph serialisation (GraphML) provides the best quality– latency trade-off for generation, likely due to LLM familiarity with structured syntax. Applied to 500 questions over EU banking regulations (CRR + CRD IV), the optimised GraphRAG pipeline achieves win rates of 58–67% against Naive, HyDE, and Hybrid RAG baselines across comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and correctness. All generation components use open-source LLMs (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct), and datasets are publicly available, supporting reproducibility.

title: Machine Learning Algorithms for Credit Card Fraud Detection: Cost-Sensitive Evaluation and Model Selection
abstract: Abstract The rise in online transactions has made credit card fraud a significant global concern, necessitating detection strategies that are both highly accurate and practically viable. While existing literature extensively explores machine learning techniques to address class imbalance, most studies optimize for traditional statistical metrics, overlooking the asymmetric financial costs and strict operational constraints of real-world fraud detection. This study bridges this gap by proposing a comprehensive, cost-sensitive ensemble framework evaluated on a real-world European cardholder dataset. We move beyond the traditional F 1 score by adopting the cost-sensitive F β metric to reflect real financial impact. Through exhaustive benchmarking, we show that while eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) combined with Borderline SMOTE achieves the highest single-model performance, our proposed soft-voting ensemble integrating Logistic Regression and Random Forest with SMOTE delivers the best overall performance ( F β = 0.8287). To ensure practical viability, we introduce a Top- K operational constraint evaluation reflecting limited human investigation bandwidths. Additionally, an ablation study demonstrates that there is no universal remedy for class imbalance; optimal interventions are highly model-dependent. Finally, by validating our framework on a feature-transparent simulated dataset, model interpretability analysis reveals the ensemble’s capacity to capture the critical importance of environmental risk factors, shifting the focus beyond solely customer-centric anomalies.

title: BuildGraph: A Synthetic Multi-Archetype Building Knowledge Graph Dataset
abstract: Semantic querying of building knowledge graphs (KGs) underpins the integration of artificial intelligence into building operations, from natural-language access to cross-building analytics, but such KGs are rarely public owing to proprietary, security, and cost barriers. BuildGraph is a synthetic building KG dataset of 120 buildings in the Brick Schema ontology, grounded in U.S. Department of Energy prototype models and sensor-placement patterns from real buildings. It spans eight commercial building types across three ASHRAE energy-code vintages, with five realizations per archetype varying URI naming, sensor-attachment predicates, and topology. A 75-query SPARQL benchmark confirms structural completeness: BuildGraph reaches 91.5% Query Answerability Rate versus 35.8% for 59 real-world Brick files. Independently, it reproduces real buildings' sensor-type proportions on their shared vocabulary (cosine 0.86-0.94), evidence of realistic instrumentation where measurable. A downstream text-to-SPARQL experiment with Gemma 4 (26B) reaches 27.3% Row-Matching F1 (+17.5 pp over zero-shot) on 12 held-out buildings. BuildGraph gives facility managers and digital-twin developers a testbed for portable analytics and natural-language interfaces, and its dataset, generator, and benchmark are openly available at https://github.com/humanbuildingsynergy/BuildGraph.

evidence.title: BuildGraph: A Synthetic Multi-Archetype Building Knowledge Graph Dataset
evidence.abstract: BuildGraph is a dataset of 120 commercial building knowledge graphs in the Brick Schema ontology (v1.3), provided as RDF Turtle (.ttl) files. Buildings are parameterized from U.S. DOE Commercial Prototype Building Models across 8 building types (small office, medium office, large office, primary school, hospital, hotel, strip mall, outpatient healthcare) and 3 ASHRAE 90.1 energy code vintages (pre-1980, 2004, 2013), yielding 24 archetypes × 5 random seeds = 120 buildings. Sensor placement probabilities are calibrated against 1,421 patterns mined from 65 real commercial buildings on the Mortar platform, included in this deposit as empirical_patterns.json. Each building independently samples a sensor-attachment style (brick:hasPoint / brick:isPointOf / both) and a URI naming convention (numeric, hyphenated, descriptive, or legacy), mirroring heterogeneity found in real deployed Brick buildings. Dataset scale ranges from ~100 triples (sparse pre-1980 strip mall) to ~11,000 triples (dense 2013 hotel), with a mean of 1,865 triples and 470 typed entities per building. This deposit also includes sparql_queries.json, a benchmark of 75 SPARQL queries across 5 categories (equipment discovery, sensor/point relations, topological traversal, aggregation, multi-hop/complex) with automatic scope detection. BuildGraph buildings achieve an overall Query Answerability Rate (QAR) of 91.5% on this benchmark, compared to 35.8% for 59 publicly available real-world Brick building files. The generator code and benchmark scripts are available at https://github.com/humanbuildingsynergy/BuildGraph.

title: Who Speaks for the Pruned? Visual Token Pruning as Coverage Optimization
abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of vision-language models (VLMs), but most methods only ask which tokens to keep. This retained-token view can keep redundant high-scoring tokens while leaving discarded evidence without a close representative. We propose CoverPruner, a training-free pruner that asks the complementary demand-side question: after a token is removed, which surviving original token represents it for the target VLM? CoverPruner formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM), covering the full projected visual-token set with query-weighted demand. It instantiates RCM with projector-space coverage and a lightweight first-layer attention probe. Across multiple VLM architectures and compression rates, CoverPruner achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods, with the largest gains usually appearing under aggressive compression.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Adverse Weather Restoration via Gated Transformer Network
abstract: Restoring images degraded by adverse weather remains challenging due to spatially heterogeneous degradations. Many existing weather-specific restoration models rely on weather-agnostic global aggregation, naive cross-scale fusion, and deterministic objectives, which struggle to handle heterogeneous degradations in all-in-one adverse-weather settings. To address these limitations, we propose an Uncertainty-guided Adverse-weather Restoration Network (UAR-Net), a weather-specific AiO framework that integrates a gated transformer with balanced multi-scale skip connections. Specifically, we employ Gated Dual-scale Transformer Blocks (GDTB) to jointly model selective global interactions and multi-scale local structures, a progressive Balanced Multi-scale Skip Connection (BMSC) for balanced multi-scale feature integration, and an Uncertainty-Aware Refinement Head (URH) that performs artifact removal, detail enhancement, and predictive uncertainty estimation. The model is supervised by a Brightness-Aware Energy Loss (BAE-Loss) to encourage accurate reconstruction with well-calibrated uncertainty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple adverse-weather benchmarks. The codes will open source upon acceptance.

title: Type-Directed, Secure-by-Construction Enclave Partitioning for LLVM
abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware-supported isolation through enclaves that protect code and data independently of software abstractions. However, TEEs alone cannot enforce information-flow security. This problem is further aggravated in LLVM-like low-level languages that allow unrestricted pointer manipulation and unstructured control flow. Moreover, using TEEs effectively typically requires manually partitioning applications into enclave and non-enclave components, a process that is labor-intensive, error-prone, and lacks fine-grained control. We address these challenges with a three-step approach. First, we formalize SIR, an enclave-oblivious calculus based on LLVM IR, equipped with a novel permissive type system that enforces security against low-level attackers. To obtain meaningful guarantees, SIR combines information-flow control with security-aware coarse-grained memory safety. Second, we extend SIR to SIREN, an enclave-aware calculus that enforces noninterference against stronger attackers capable of observing arbitrary non-enclave memory. Third, we develop a type-driven, type-preserving compilation from SIR to SIREN that automatically produces secure enclave-aware programs, eliminating manual partitioning while providing fine-grained control over host-enclave boundaries. We implement and evaluate SPLITR on thirteen microbenchmarks and real-world workloads, including applications from SGXGauge, on Intel SGX hardware. SPLITR scales to OpenSSL (425,953 LLVM IR instructions) and supports multiple objectives that expose trade-offs among enclave TCB size, host-enclave transitions, and boundary data movement. For OpenSSL, optimizing for transitions reduces them from 393 to 187. Runtime overhead is dominated by fixed enclave costs for short-running workloads, whereas long-running applications better amortize these costs and approach native performance.

title: Efficient Sensor Fusion Through Covariance-Constrained Observation Decimation (CCOD)
abstract: Observation decimation is frequently employed in state estimation to reduce sensing, communication, and computational requirements, but decreasing the measurement assimilation frequency increases estimation uncertainty. Selecting an appropriate observation decimation factor therefore requires accurately predicting the resulting estimator performance. While the discrete algebraic Riccati equation (DARE) provides the steady-state estimation-error covariance for standard linear time-invariant Kalman filters, it is not directly applicable to estimators employing decimated measurement updates. Existing approaches address this limitation through lifted system representations or periodic Riccati equation formulations, both of which incur additional computational complexity. This paper presents a covariance-constrained observation decimation (CCOD) framework that reformulates the DARE inputs using equivalent decimated system and process-noise matrices that capture covariance growth between measurement updates. The proposed reformulation enables direct prediction of the steady-state estimation-error covariance through a single DARE evaluation without increasing the system dimension or solving coupled periodic Riccati equations. The resulting covariance prediction is used to determine the maximum observation decimation factor that satisfies a prescribed estimation uncertainty bound. Validation using a high dimensional linear time-invariant system and a space object tracking application demonstrates that the proposed approach accurately predicts steady-state estimator performance while reducing the measurement assimilation frequency required to satisfy specified covariance constraints.

title: CAHR-Net: Condition-Adaptive Hysteresis Reconstruction for Compact and Interpretable Magnetic Core Loss Modeling
abstract: Magnetic core loss originates in the hysteresis loop: the energy dissipated per excitation cycle equals the loop area, and frequency, temperature, and waveform shape set the loss by reshaping the loop geometry. Most existing models let these conditions act only on a terminal scalar - empirical equations fold them into fitted exponents, and data-driven predictors append them to encoded features - so no intermediate hysteresis representation remains for the conditions to reshape. This paper proposes CAHR-Net, a condition-adaptive hysteresis reconstruction network that injects the operating conditions where they physically act. It preserves the interpretable chain from flux density waveform to magnetic field reconstruction, loop-area integration, and power loss estimation, and uses feature-wise linear modulation to inject frequency, temperature, and waveform statistics into the intermediate reconstruction representation. A matched large-batch training protocol based on AdamW, cosine scheduling, and a staged reconstruction-to-power-loss objective is also reported, because the modulation pathway takes effect only within it. On the MagNet final A-E material protocol, CAHR-Net attains an average p95 relative error of 6.89% with only 1874 parameters, the lowest among all compared methods, together with a lower worst-material p95 than the strongest black-box solution at about 48x fewer parameters; it reduces the average p95 of the physical reconstruction backbone from 7.47% to 6.89% and the p95 of material D, the most difficult material, from 16.40% to 14.87%. Ablation and condition-slice analyses attribute the improvement to the coupling of physical loop reconstruction, structured condition modulation, and the matched optimization trajectory.

title: Probability Logic and Adaptive Optimization of Nonlinear Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of probability logic to the optimization of nonlinear systems, specifically focusing on the development of an adaptive optimization method that dynamically adjusts to system changes. Traditional optimization techniques often rely on predefined objective functions, limiting their adaptability to dynamic environments. This work proposes a novel approach that integrates probabilistic models directly into the optimization algorithm, enabling the system to adjust optimization parameters based on probabilistic distributions. The core mechanism involves embedding probability models to dynamically steer the optimization process, offering potential improvements in performance and robustness in complex systems. We present a preliminary investigation showcasing the effectiveness of this method in a simulated scenario, demonstrating its ability to adapt to changing input parameters and achieve optimal solutions with enhanced resilience.

title: Silent failure and repair of the quantum component in hybrid quantum–classical models — code, results and pre-registration files
abstract: This archive accompanies the manuscript "Silent failure and repair of the quantum component in hybrid quantum–classical models" (Şahin & Mert, submitted). It contains the complete code, per-run results, per-run logits, pre-registered analysis plans and the discrepancy index from which every number in the paper is generated; no value in the manuscript is entered by hand. Contents: - code/ — original training pipeline (v7.1), re-analysis and diagnosis scripts (Round 4), repair and pre-specified confirmation campaign (Round 5), pre-submission hardening (Round 6), and the figure / Supplementary Information / manuscript builders - results/ — per-run CSV files and generated summaries for every round, per-run logit arrays for the repaired-design campaign, and the paper figures (600 DPI) - prereg/ — analysis plans and decision rules written before the corresponding runs (HUNT_PLAN.md, RUN_ORDER_*.md) - audit/ — discrepancy index (nothing deleted; superseded entries marked), round reports, and the claims ledger verifying 104 numerical statements of the manuscript against source files Environment: Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.10, Transformers 4.57, PennyLane 0.42, Optuna 4.5, statsmodels 0.14; single NVIDIA RTX 5090. Reproduction commands are in README.md. Model checkpoints (~40 GB) are not included; they are regenerated deterministically by the scripts. The App Reviews corpus used in the experiments is archived separately (see Related works).

title: 基于自适应的动态矩阵学习算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic matrix learning algorithm designed to enhance data training efficiency and accuracy. Traditional matrix learning methods often rely on static parameters, limiting their adaptability to evolving data. This paper introduces a self-adaptive algorithm that dynamically adjusts matrix parameters during training, enabling more flexible data representation and improved performance. The core mechanism involves a continuous parameter refinement process driven by a learning objective, achieved through a modified stochastic gradient descent framework. We analyze the algorithm's performance through extensive experiments, demonstrating its superior efficiency and accuracy compared to existing static matrix learning techniques. The paper concludes with a discussion of the key findings and potential future directions of the research.

title: Dynamic Quantum Superposition: A Novel Algorithmic Approach for Adaptive Quantum Computation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithmic framework for dynamic quantum superposition, termed "Dynamic Quantum Superposition," designed to enhance the versatility and efficiency of quantum computation. The core principle of this approach lies in dynamically adjusting the underlying topology of quantum superposition states, allowing for a significantly more flexible and adaptive quantum system. We present a detailed description of the algorithm's mechanism, including the mathematical formulation of the transformation applied to the state vector, and demonstrate its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation. This research explores the potential of this dynamic approach to overcome limitations of traditional quantum computation and pave the way for new computational paradigms. The algorithm's focus is on accelerating quantum computation by optimizing the state space.

title: Non-Standard Arithmetic of Quantum States
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of utilizing non-standard arithmetic to generate complex mathematical functions, leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core aim is to design a framework based on quantum entanglement that can produce sophisticated mathematical results through calculations, and exploit entanglement to enhance computational efficiency. We propose a novel approach centered around the generation of functions directly from quantum states, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical arithmetic. The paper explores the potential of this framework to enable new mathematical discoveries and algorithmic advancements. Specifically, we address the challenge of efficiently manipulating and processing information encoded within quantum states. The investigation delves into the fundamental principles of entanglement and their implications for creating a new paradigm in computational mathematics.

title: No Fixation, No Bill: Settlement Events as the Only Taxable Events in a Record Ledger
abstract: In ledger-based descriptions of measurement, a common misreading is that every inter action or correlation is “charged” by the framework. We state and prove the opposite: taxation is defined only on settlement events, and a two-chain correlation may be physically real while re maining outside the domain of the tax map. Fixation and witness count are defined as bivalent predicates built from mutual-information and fidelity measurements at declared thresholds, with concordance assigned to a majority audit. The tax rule is a cost functional undefined outside the settlement domain (type-partial), total and strictly positive on it by two declared economy axioms; the main lemma is shown to depend only on that partiality. Under explicit fairness axioms — no witness privileged by identity, no outcome privileged by content — every arbitration between two witnesses returns ⊥, while a three-witness majority satisfies both axioms and restores decidability; a coding-theoretic floor independently forces the same numeral, since single-fault correction requires code distance at least three. One canonical hardness measure is registered, normalized to Landauer erasure work. All verdicts are conditional on the declared models, thresholds, and finite statistics; the contribution is the decision procedure itself, not a model-free fact of nature. The distinction between a “zero bill” and “no bill” is structural, not numerical — and that is what protects the framework from the “universe as a toll booth” caricature.

title: Quantum Security Multi-Party Computation Based on Quantum Coherence
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum coherence, specifically quantum coherence, to enhance the security of hardware multi-party computation (MPC). Traditional MPC protocols often rely on computational assumptions that are increasingly vulnerable to advancements in classical computing power. Quantum coherence presents a fundamentally different approach to security, leveraging the ephemeral nature of quantum states to mitigate information leakage. We propose a novel MPC protocol that utilizes quantum coherence to create a secure environment where participants can collaboratively compute a function without revealing their individual inputs. The core of the protocol lies in carefully designed quantum operations and measurement strategies that exploit the inherent fragility of quantum coherence. This approach offers a promising path towards building robust and secure MPC systems suitable for applications requiring high levels of confidentiality, particularly in scenarios where classical computational attacks are a significant concern. We detail the protocol's structure, outlining the key elements and providing a mathematical framework for analyzing its security properties. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential challenges and future research directions in this emerging area.

evidence.title: Quantum Security Multi-Party Computation Based on Quantum Coherence
evidence.abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum coherence, specifically quantum coherence, to enhance the security of hardware multi-party computation (MPC). Traditional MPC protocols often rely on computational assumptions that are increasingly vulnerable to advancements in classical computing power. Quantum coherence presents a fundamentally different approach to security, leveraging the ephemeral nature of quantum states to mitigate information leakage. We propose a novel MPC protocol that utilizes quantum coherence to create a secure environment where participants can collaboratively compute a function without revealing their individual inputs. The core of the protocol lies in carefully designed quantum operations and measurement strategies that exploit the inherent fragility of quantum coherence. This approach offers a promising path towards building robust and secure MPC systems suitable for applications requiring high levels of confidentiality, particularly in scenarios where classical computational attacks are a significant concern. We detail the protocol's structure, outlining the key elements and providing a mathematical framework for analyzing its security properties. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential challenges and future research directions in this emerging area.

title: ##基于量子纠缠的分布式密钥生成协议
abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed key generation (DKG) protocol leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement. Traditional DKG protocols often rely on classical cryptographic techniques, introducing vulnerabilities to sophisticated attacks. Our protocol utilizes entangled photon pairs to establish a shared secret key between multiple parties without any prior secret sharing. The core mechanism involves the creation of an entangled state and subsequent measurements performed by the participants. The correlations inherent in quantum entanglement allow for the derivation of a shared key, guaranteeing security against eavesdropping attempts. We formally define the protocol, outlining the key parameters and security assumptions. The presented system offers a potentially more secure alternative to existing DKG methods, particularly against adversaries with access to classical communication channels. We explore the protocol's mathematical foundations, detailing the process of key generation and emphasizing the inherent security provided by the laws of quantum mechanics. This work provides a theoretical framework for a future, practical implementation of a quantum-secured DKG system.

title: Multi-Scale Neuron Models and Cognitive Mapping
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to cognitive modeling by integrating multi-scale neuron models with cognitive mapping techniques. The core idea is that complex cognitive processes can be more accurately represented by simulating them across multiple scales, ultimately forming a multi-scale cognitive map. This is achieved through the construction of hierarchical neural networks, mimicking the layered activity of neurons from the molecular level to the whole-brain level. Information theory, specifically entropy quantification, is employed to quantify the cognitive information present at each scale. The resulting models offer a more nuanced understanding of cognition and provide a framework for exploring the relationships between different cognitive processes. This work demonstrates the potential for creating a dynamic model of cognition and offers a method for characterizing the information content within it.

title: 基于领域自适应迁移学习的机器人控制
abstract: This paper investigates the application of domain adaptation for transfer learning in robotic control. The core challenge in deploying robots across diverse environments is their sensitivity to variations in these environments. Traditional control methods often require extensive retraining for each new domain, which is both time-consuming and computationally expensive. This research proposes a framework utilizing domain adaptation techniques to effectively transfer a control model from a source domain to a target domain. The framework leverages domain adaptation algorithms to learn domain-specific features and adjust model parameters, thereby enhancing the robot's adaptability and robustness. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline a structured methodology for implementation. The key contribution lies in the systematic application of domain adaptation to robotics, offering a robust solution for real-world deployment scenarios. The overall goal is to reduce the reliance on extensive domain-specific data collection and significantly improve the generalization capabilities of robotic control systems.

title: 基于动态几何拓扑的自适应量子态生成
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state generation algorithm based on dynamic geometric topology. Traditional quantum state generation methods typically rely on static parameters, but this approach leverages dynamic geometric topology to generate quantum states with complex topological structures, thereby enhancing quantum computation efficiency. The algorithm employs a series of iterative transformations that map initial quantum states into a complex topological space, resulting in a diverse range of quantum states. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through simulations and analysis, showcasing improved quantum state diversity and efficiency compared to existing techniques. The core mechanism centers on the construction and manipulation of topological spaces, enabling the generation of highly intricate and controllable quantum states.

title: Title: Adaptive Constraint Relaxation in Dynamic Neural Networks
abstract: Adaptive Constraint Relaxation in Dynamic Neural Networks addresses the challenges of generalization and robustness in neural networks by introducing a novel adaptive relaxation mechanism. This mechanism dynamically adjusts constraint strength based on observation data, ensuring the network's ability to generalize to unseen data. The core concept is a 'flow-based' relaxation algorithm that continuously monitors the network's output and optimizes constraint parameters. This approach offers a more flexible and robust method compared to traditional constraint-based techniques, potentially leading to improved performance on diverse datasets. This paper presents a detailed theoretical analysis and practical implementation of this algorithm, demonstrating its effectiveness through simulations and preliminary experiments. We evaluate the algorithm's performance across various benchmark datasets, showcasing its ability to enhance generalization and robustness.

title: ##基于量子纠错码的容错硬件设计
abstract: This paper presents a hardware design leveraging quantum error correction (QEC) codes for enhanced fault tolerance in quantum computing. Current approaches to QEC primarily rely on software-based correction, limiting the practical implementation of robust quantum systems. This design proposes an architecture where QEC codes are directly integrated into the hardware circuit design, capitalizing on the inherent error-correcting capabilities of the codes themselves. The core mechanism involves encoding quantum information using specific QEC codes, performing logical operations, and then decoding the results to mitigate errors. This approach aims to significantly improve the accuracy and reliability of quantum computations by directly addressing errors at the hardware level. The design focuses on practical considerations for implementing QEC codes within a physical quantum system, exploring key challenges and potential solutions. This work contributes to the development of more reliable and scalable quantum computing platforms.

title: Synthetic Data in a Data-Intensive World: A Literature Review to Address an Application-Driven Analysis
abstract: Synthetic data are increasing their popularity in different disciplines. Indeed, in addition to their affordability, synthetic data may play an effective protective role to address privacy issues, which are extremely critical in certain application domains such as healthcare, as well as they represent a relatively simple solution to overcome access restrictions. However, despite synthetic data are not a novelty and their potentialities in the different domains have been largely discussed, their operationalization and utility are still object of research. More recently, the unprecedented AI capabilities have naturally enabled and quickly consolidated a feedback loop, where synthetic data is, at the same time, a valuable resource to further develop and refine technology, as well as an added, often critical, value within the different application domains. By combining hybrid retrieval and analysis techniques, 250+ relevant papers have been selected, classified and analyzed. In a context of discussion about legal, ethical and political implications amid opportunities and challenges, the review has clearly pointed out a need for a more consolidated engineering approach to synthetic data as a response to the intrinsic complexity of applications in the current technological climate.

title: Optimization design of contact spring based on improved marine predators algorithm
abstract: To meet the technical requirements of compactness and high performance for equipment in new power systems, this paper addresses the critical issues of large volume and inadequate breaking performance in low-voltage circuit breakers. A mathematical model for miniaturization is established by fully considering the constraint conditions of contact springs, such as structural strength, elastic force, and installation space. An enhanced Marine Predators Algorithm (ETMPA) is proposed for optimal solution: it introduces an elite opposition-based learning strategy to enrich population diversity and strengthen global search capability, while integrating a t-distribution disturbance strategy to improve individuals’ ability to escape local optima in the late iteration stage. Experimental results demonstrate that ETMPA effectively reduces the mass and volume of contact springs without compromising functional performance, successfully achieving the miniaturization of low-voltage circuit breakers. This research provides valuable technical support for equipment upgrading and transformation in automated scenarios of new power systems, promoting the development of efficient and compact electrical equipment.

title: Dual-Latent Memory Routing for Vision-Language Reasoning
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have recently made strong progress in vision-language reasoning, yet their performance often degrades as generations grow longer. A key factor is that they frequently lose track of earlier visual evidence and intermediate constraints under a monolithic growing context. Inspired by how humans separately recall what they see and what they infer when solving complex tasks, we propose DLMR, a parameter-efficient mechanism that equips MLLMs with Dual Latent Memories: a visual memory that compresses image evidence and a reasoning memory that tracks intermediate conclusions and constraints. A Router then dynamically decides which memory and how much to reuse during inference, preserving visual grounding while maintaining coherent long-horizon reasoning. DLMR is trained in three stages, from latent memory construction to selective router learning, while keeping the base MLLM frozen, yielding substantial gains on both general and reasoning benchmarks with only a small number of additional trainable parameters. Analyses further show interpretable, state-dependent routing with specialized memory roles and reduced decoding tokens over long generations. Code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-Wrynn/DLMR.

title: Neural operators approximate strongly continuous convex monotone semigroups
abstract: We approximate strongly continuous convex monotone semigroups by learning their Chernoff-type one-step operators with neural operators. First, we introduce the general class of so-called Chernoff-neural operators and show in a universal approximation theorem that they can approximate the Chernoff one-step operators arbitrarily well. By using stability estimates between weighted Hölder spaces, the one-step approximation error can be propagated through the iterations which yields universal approximation of the corresponding semigroup. Second, we introduce the more specialized class of envelope-neural operators for envelope semigroups which allows us to derive quantitative approximation rates. Finally, we illustrate the effectiveness of these neural operators in several numerical examples arising from non-linear partial differential equations, stochastic optimal control and stochastic processes under model uncertainty.

title: Prototype-guided transfer of sparse literature knowledge for electrolyte additive discovery
abstract: Electrolyte additive discovery remains challenging because experimentally validated molecules are sparse, whereas accessible chemical spaces are vast and largely unlabeled. This challenge is amplified in lithium-ion batteries, where additive performance arises from coupled interfacial reactions rather than a single molecular property. Here, we develop a prototype-guided molecular intelligence, ProtoMI, a literature-driven framework that learns transferable structural priors from reported electrolyte additives and uses them to prioritize candidates in unlabeled chemical space. For boron-containing additives, ProtoMI combines 126 literature-reported molecules with 179,977 unlabeled candidates. Graph contrastive learning identifies seven chemically interpretable prototypes from the reported additives, and prototype guided semi-supervised contrastive learning adapts these prototypes to the candidate space under source-target distribution mismatch. In retrospective temporal validation, ProtoMI achieves enrichment factors of 9.2-45.6 while screening less than 2% of the candidate space. A subsequent translation step identifies four commercially accessible candidates. One representative candidate, 4,4,5,5-Tetramethyl-2-[10-(1naphthyl)anthracen-9-yl]-1,3,2-dioxaborolane (TNDB), improves high-temperature LiFePO4||graphite cycling at 55 °C by 34.93% relative to the baseline electrolyte. An arsenal of characterizations and operando optical fiber Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy suggest that TNDB forms B-containing, F/P/O-modified inorganic interphases, suppresses solvent decomposition and reduces Fe deposition on graphite. This case study shows how sparse literature knowledge can guide experimentally efficient molecular discovery in data-scarce battery-additive spaces.

title: AutoCompass: Accurate Visual Localization on Public Maps by Learning from Weak Labels
abstract: Neural map matchers estimate an image's 3-DoF pose relative to a 2D map. These models are trained on large-scale datasets of geo-referenced images, whose position and heading labels often contain noise that affects the trained models. To address this, we present AutoCompass, a supervision approach for training neural map matchers from inaccurate absolute pose labels. First, we show that heading labels are unnecessary: trained from raw GPS labels, models learn to predict accurate headings, automatically. Second, defining a tolerance region around raw GPS improves positional accuracy. Third, if available, our supervision uses relative poses between training images, obtained via SLAM or SfM, which provide a more accurate training signal. Across driving and egocentric benchmarks, AutoCompass consistently outperforms counterparts trained with the usual strong reliance on absolute pose labels.

title: SelfLift: Accelerating Few-Step Diffusion via Self-Recovering Resolution Transition
abstract: Few-step diffusion models substantially compress temporal computation, making the spatial cost of each model evaluation an increasingly dominant source of inference latency. Progressive-resolution inference reduces this cost by performing early denoising at low resolution and reserving high-resolution computation for refinement. However, existing methods typically lift intermediate latents directly and rely on subsequent steps to absorb the induced distribution mismatch. In the few-step regime, the limited recovery budget leaves these errors as visible artifacts, constraining how late the transition can occur and, consequently, how efficiently it can be performed. We introduce SelfLift, a self-recovering progressive-resolution framework that derives both transition-repair signals and trajectory-aligned supervision from the generative model itself. SelfLift-zero proposes a training-free Artifact-Aware Consistency Lift, using disagreement between direct latent lifting and pixel-VAE re-encoding as both a localized artifact-risk signal and a model-native correction direction. It enables reliable late transitions without external super-resolution, extra denoiser evaluations, or sampling-schedule modifications. Building on this robust transition, SelfLift-rich performs On-Policy Self Recovery on student-visited states, transferring dense high-resolution guidance from an internal self-teacher while remaining aligned with the altered progressive-resolution dynamics. Across FLUX.2-Klein and Z-Image-Turbo, SelfLift reduces end-to-end latency by 41.5% and 44.1%, respectively. Combined with timestep distillation, it delivers overall speedups of 29.61x and 19.21x over the corresponding 50-step models while preserving competitive generation quality, establishing a stronger speed-quality frontier for few-step diffusion.
